analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks with up to $50 billion in assets from Dodd-Frank swap, debit-fee, and trading rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015, with zero cosponsors [S4][S5].
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would loosen three Dodd-Frank-era rules for banks with up to $50 billion in assets. It would exempt banks that size from the requirement to post collateral on interest rate swaps [S3], lift the cap on debit card swipe fees so banks between $10 billion and $50 billion could charge merchants more [S3], and let those banks keep swap trading inside the bank instead of moving it to a separate affiliate [S3]. It was referred to two House committees but never got a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, banks with between $10 billion and $50 billion in assets would have gained on all three fronts: no margin collateral on interest rate swaps [S3], freedom to charge merchants higher debit card interchange fees by clearing the Durbin amendment's $10 billion exemption threshold [S3], and no requirement to move swap trading out of the bank into a separate affiliate [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold from $10 billion to $50 billion in the swap rules, so banks far larger than community banks escape margin requirements on interest rate swaps [S3].

Amends the Electronic Fund Transfer Act so insured depository institutions and credit unions with up to $50 billion in assets are carved out of the debit interchange fee limit, letting them charge merchants higher swipe fees [S3].
Amends Dodd-Frank Section 165(i) so only banks with $50 billion or more in assets must conduct covered swap activities outside the bank, sparing smaller ones the push-out requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Merchants would bear higher debit card fees, which typically get passed to shoppers through prices; and removing margin requirements for a wider set of swap dealers would put more uncollateralized risk into the derivatives system, which the public ultimately backstops [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Merchants, shoppers, and the financial system

drawbacks.text: Raising the debit fee exemption from $10 billion to $50 billion would let mid-sized banks charge retailers higher swipe fees on everyday card purchases, a cost that flows to merchants and consumers [S3].
Exempting banks up to $50 billion from swap margin rules weakens a post-2008 safeguard designed to make sure derivatives dealers post collateral, increasing risk in the financial system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is pitched as relief for community banks, but it moves the exemption line fivefold, from $10 billion to $50 billion, so its main beneficiaries are regional banks many times the size of a community bank. The gains for those banks come partly at the direct expense of merchants and card users through higher debit fees, and partly at the expense of systemic safeguards. It died without a vote, so its costs were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2014 and referred to the Financial Services and Agriculture committees, then to a subcommittee in July, but no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Duffy (R-WI) introduced the bill on May 30, 2014 [S1].
It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On July 7, 2014, the portion under Agriculture's jurisdiction was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, merchants and card users avoided the higher debit swipe fees it would have allowed, and the post-2008 swap safeguards stayed intact. Mid-sized banks, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Merchants and card users kept lower fees

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise Dodd-Frank exemption thresholds to $50 billion for mid-sized banks.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it was never reported out or scheduled for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split exists in the record; the sponsor was a Republican and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would free these banks from swap margin rules, from moving swap trading outside the bank, and from the debit swipe fee cap. Its clearest gain to them — higher debit interchange fees — is paid by merchants and, in practice, by consumers.
Merchants pay debit interchange fees on every card sale; letting banks up to $50 billion escape the fee cap would raise their costs, typically passed on to shoppers in prices.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions (under $10 billion)
industries.note: They were already exempt or covered by existing consideration-for-exemption language, so the bill mainly helps banks well above their size; it does little for genuinely small lenders despite the 'Main Street' name.
